Lessons.Title: Represent Products as Areas — Multiplication with Unit Squares
ExplanationParagraphs: First-edition IM K–5 2021 Grade 3 Unit 2 Lesson 5, source standard 3.MD.C.7.b. Learners connect products with rectangles completely covered by equal-size square units: the number of rows times the squares per row is the covered area. The original learner PDF is four pages, including 7 original image-card matches and 5 separately drawn rectangles. Edulytics supplies independently authored cards preserving mathematical dimensions, not publisher artwork.

Warm-up 'How Many Do You See: One More' (10 minutes). Original figure 1 depicts FIVE separate groups of three dots, 15 altogether. Figure 2 depicts SIX groups of three, 18 altogether. Figure 3 depicts SIX clusters of FOUR dots, each four-dot cluster being a 2×2 mini-array, 24 total. The third figure has been visually source-verified, not inferred from an incomplete alt string. Flash each figure, solicit row/group strategies and ask how one extra group changes the known total. Teacher checks verbal reasoning and MP7 structure.

Activity 1 'Match Expressions and Areas' (15 minutes): source teacher posts seven 2021 grid-based original blackline cards around the room. The original seven-page publisher blackline source was individually inspected. Their exact mathematical labels and dimensions are A=2 rows×6 columns=12, B=5×7=35, C=8×2=16, D=3×3=9, E=7×10=70, F=9×5=45, G=8×4=32. These cards are independently redrawn in Edulytics using generic CSS square cells, without copying published artwork.

The seven public source expressions, presented in original order, map to FIRST-PARTY card letters as follows: 9×5→F; 8×2→C; 7×10→E; 3×3→D; 2×6→A; 8×4→G; 5×7→B. Learners identify ONE card for each and explain how the source factors describe two side lengths. The card-letter grader checks only the selected letter. The teacher must review actual equal square geometry and explanation of rows, columns and area. Before independent card matching the teacher models a 5×3=15 tile grid and records multiple legitimate ways to describe it.

Activity 2 'Create from Expressions' (20 minutes): each learner uses blank unit-square grid paper (and optionally inch tiles) to DRAW, label and find area for all five source expressions: (a) 3×4=12, (b) 4×6=24, (c) 6×3=18, (d) 7×4=28, (e) 3×2=6 square units. The original student PDF part 2 separately asks why multiplication finds rectangular area. The teacher may differentiate by inviting a suitable learner to select at least three of the five. The completeness claim is about all FIVE task records, not about requiring every differentiated student to finish all five.

Source Activity 2 Engagement: provide choice in difficulty, allow square-inch tiles if useful, compare two students' differently oriented rectangles for the same expression. This lesson assesses AREA OF SPACE and not merely an array of dots. Peer talk explains how factors describe the numbers of rows or columns and squares per row or column; grading a numeric product alone cannot certify a correctly drawn/tiled region.

Lesson synthesis uses a genuine 2021 2×7 rectangle containing fourteen congruent square units and labels the sides 2 and 7. Ask whether 2×7 and 7×2 each count the same tiled region, and distinguish tiled AREA from separate objects in arrays. Teacher preparation reflects on students' prior array understanding. Optional centers in the 2021 source are Capture Squares Stage 6 (multiply with 1–5) and Rectangle Rumble Stage 1 (factors 1, 2, 5 and 10).

The 2021 publisher's gated 'Create a Rectangular Area' Cool-down is not reproduced. The Edulytics separately authored 6×5=30 square-unit diagram task is source-goal equivalent only. Source printed cards and copyrighted illustrations are not redistributed. Rich V2 is provided as first-party canonical authoring material; tests/CI, materialized database runtime and academic acceptance are separately deferred Stage D.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rows × columns measure area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each fully covered congruent square cell is one square unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count rows of equal-sized square units, then multiply by number in each row.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal units are essential
KeyConcepts.Definition: Product-as-area applies when square cells cover the region with no gaps or overlap.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A group of dots alone counts objects; filled squares count covered space.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two objects cannot be identified as two square units without a defined square region.

KeyConcepts.Title: Source-equivalent matching cards
KeyConcepts.Definition: Seven independently redrawn area cards A–G each represent a source-original rectangle dimension.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a source factor pair to find the tile configuration; justify the MATCH, not just the total.
KeyConcepts.Example: Original card F has 9 rows of 5 tiles; 9×5=45.

KeyConcepts.Title: Commutative rectangular orientation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Reversing row/column factor order does not change area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A 3×6 drawing and a 6×3 drawing have 18 units each when unit size is the same.
KeyConcepts.Example: Count 18 square units in either orientation.

KeyConcepts.Title: A checked numeric product is partial evidence
KeyConcepts.Definition: A learner may compute area correctly without constructing or matching the required source diagram.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Teacher reviews drawings, materials, labelling and unit interpretation.
KeyConcepts.Example: Writing 12 is not equivalent to drawing a complete 3×4 grid.

WorkedExamples.Title: First-edition image progression
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain how 15, 18 and 24 arise from original source warm-ups.
Steps: Six clusters containing four dots each: 6×4=24.
Explain how the additional group or larger cluster changes the total.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks actual six-cluster grouping and explanatory reasoning.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check all seven original source card matches
WorkedExamples.Question: Which original source-equivalent A–G image matches each expression?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare grid rows/columns and map each expression to matching first-party card.
Steps: For EACH source expression, explain the two side lengths and covered unit squares.
WorkedExamples.Answer: F, C, E, D, A, G, B
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher validates interpretation of first-party grid; numeric or letter feedback cannot score human explanation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Draw five separate rectangle areas
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the area of 3×4, 4×6, 6×3, 7×4 and 3×2.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw separately on congruent square grid, label side lengths and multiply.
Steps: Explain that each complete row contributes one equal number of square units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every drawing must be checked; source allows teacher differentiation to three of five when warranted.

WorkedExamples.Title: Area instead of number of dots
WorkedExamples.Question: Why is a 2×7 grid said to have 14 square units?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use identical contiguous square tiles filling a rectangle.
Steps: Draw two rows each containing seven unit squares.
Count 14 full square regions with no gaps or overlap.
Rotate the array and count seven rows of two.
Describe the measured two-dimensional area rather than just objects.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews area units, representation and alternative grouping.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling the third 2021 warm-up figure unknown or using six groups of three again.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The third original image contains six distinct 2×2 clusters, four dots per cluster.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count 6×4=24; cite group size and six groups.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Matching an original 5×7 rectangle to a 7×4 grid.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Those have 35 and 28 unit squares respectively.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Original B is 5×7; seven-card matches are F,C,E,D,A,G,B in source expression order.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating row length only as area.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Area depends on both independent counts, rows and columns.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count the complete unit square regions in the grid and multiply.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using correct numeric products as proof of correctly drawn area rectangles.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source asks for separately drawn, labelled rectangles and justifications, not scalar answers.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Apply numeric feedback plus mandatory teacher geometric review.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing source 2×7 tile space with 14 separated objects.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source synthesis deliberately contrasts separate object arrays with tiled area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State square units and the condition of no gaps or overlaps.

SummaryPoints: 2021 four-page original Student Task Statements PDF, six lesson-page figures and seven-page A–G source blackline cards were individually inspected.
Warm-ups: 5×3=15, 6×3=18, 6×4=24; third original visual has six clusters of four.
Original seven card geometry: A 2×6, B 5×7, C 8×2, D 3×3, E 7×10, F 9×5, G 8×4.
One-to-one seven source expression matches: F, C, E, D, A, G, B.
Five distinct learner-drawn rectangles: 3×4, 4×6, 6×3, 7×4, 3×2. Numeric results alone do not certify actual drawings.
Area is covered space measured by congruent square units, unlike an array of separate objects.
Original copyrighted cards are not reproduced; independent Edulytics equivalents preserve mathematical structure. The publisher's educator-gated Cool-down remains distinct.
Tests and CI not run, actual learner materialization and Stage D not started.
